result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of public spaces, and how we carry entire worlds through them without ever quite touching.

---

There's a particular quality to the light in hospital waiting rooms at six in the morning. Not the fluorescent hum of midday, but that liminal gray seeping through windows that haven't been cleaned in months, mixing with the pale glow of vending machines and the occasional blink of a printer somewhere down the hall. I've spent enough time in these spaces to know their secret architecture. The chair in the corner with the slightly broken armrest that no one fixes because everyone learns to avoid it. The water fountain that runs too cold, then too warm, never quite right. The way people arrange themselves with careful geometry—never too close, never too far, a human tessellation of privacy and need.

I used to think these were dead spaces, intervals between meaningful action. Now I think they're among the most honest places we build.

Last month I sat in one such room while my father underwent a procedure I couldn't pronounce. Across from me, a woman in her seventies held a purse the size of a small suitcase on her lap, both hands wrapped around its handle like she was holding a life preserver. She wore a coat too heavy for the heated room. Every few minutes, she'd check her phone, though it never lit up, and I'd realize she was checking the time on a phone that had died hours ago. She wasn't waiting for news—she was waiting for the shape of waiting itself to become bearable.

Three seats down, a man in construction boots scrolled through what looked like fishing videos, the sound leaking faintly from his earbuds. He laughed once, caught himself, looked around with something like guilt. As if joy had no place here, as if his waiting were somehow less legitimate if he didn't suffer it properly. I wanted to tell him that the fish jumping from green water, the brief arc of silver against sky, was as real as anything happening behind those swinging doors. That we survive these hours however we can, and survival is never improper.

But we don't talk in these rooms. That's the rule, unwritten, more powerful than any posted sign. We share oxygen, sometimes coffee from the same machine, the occasional glance of mutual recognition when something beeps too loudly or a child cries in a corridor we can't see. We are temporary neighbors in a temporary city, bound by the thinnest thread of circumstance.

What strikes me, always, is the luggage people carry. Not the bags and coats, but the visible weight of what they've brought with them into this moment. The woman with the dead phone—later I saw her pull a photograph from her wallet, just a glimpse, a young man in a military uniform, and I understood the coat, the purse, the way she held herself like something that might shatter if moved too quickly. The construction worker, I learned from a phone call he took outside (voice carrying through the thin walls), was waiting for his daughter, not his wife as I'd assumed. The fishing videos were something they'd watched together when she was small, before the thing that brought them here.

We are never just the person visible in the waiting room. We are holograms, every part of us present simultaneously—the child who learned to fear hospitals, the adult who learned to navigate them, the parent or child or friend whose fate has brought us to this particular chair at this particular hour. The body sits in fluorescent gray, but the mind travels everywhere, assembling and reassembling the narrative that explains how we arrived here, what we might say when the doctor appears, what we will do if the news is bad, what we will do if the news is good, the strange anticlimax of relief that sometimes feels almost like disappointment because at least worry had the virtue of keeping us busy.

I write this now from a different waiting room, different city, different light. The pandemic changed these spaces, or maybe just revealed what was always true. More emptiness between bodies. Masks that hide the lower half of faces, making eyes perform double duty. The anxiety of proximity in a place designed for proximity. And yet the essential grammar remains. The woman who knits with fierce concentration. The teenager who sleeps with their head against a parent's shoulder. The man who walks the same loop through the room, past the fish tank, past the reception desk, past the locked door to the restricted area, back to his seat, then up again, as if movement could hurry time itself.

I've started to collect these moments the way others collect stamps or birdsong. Not because they're beautiful, though sometimes they are. Because they represent something I can't name precisely—a form of attention, maybe, or a particular quality of being present without being seen. In waiting rooms, we are radically unperformed. No one is watching, or everyone is, but anonymously, without consequence. The social self loosens its grip. Faces settle into their true shapes. We become, briefly, more purely ourselves than we allow in the constructed world outside.

My father came through his procedure. The doctor used the word "successful" and I felt my own face change, felt the mask do nothing to hide whatever passed through my eyes. The woman with the photograph was gone by then, her seat taken by someone else. The construction worker had left during a shift change, slipping out while I was in the bathroom. I never learned his daughter's outcome. I think of them sometimes, the way you think of characters in a novel you never finished, wondering if the plot resolved or simply continued beyond the reach of your attention.

That's the thing about waiting rooms, about all these public intimacies. They don't resolve. They simply continue, a perpetual motion machine of human need and human waiting. The chairs fill and empty. The vending machine runs out of things and is restocked. The light changes incrementally through the day, and no one notices because no one is there to notice, or rather, everyone is there but noticing something else entirely—their own particular weight, their own particular wait.

I keep coming back to that morning light. How it made everyone look like photographs of themselves, slightly faded, slightly unreal. How it held us all in temporary suspension, neither here nor there, alive in the space between what we feared and what we hoped. How we were, for those hours, a community of strangers, bound by nothing except the shared fact of not yet knowing.

There's something sacred in that, I think. Something worth writing toward, even if I can't quite reach it. The way we endure uncertainty together, separately. The way we keep our dead phones charged with nothing but habit, our photographs close, our fishing videos ready. The way we sit, and wait, and survive the sitting and the waiting, and emerge eventually into whatever comes next, carrying our invisible luggage out through automatic doors, into weather, into the ongoing project of being human among other humans, all of us waiting for something, all of us here, all of us somehow, impossibly, together.

---
